conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you’ve been having worsening dry heaves and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been nonstop. I’m dry heaving many times a day now. I’m scared I’m not getting any nutrition in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Since your G-tube was removed, have you been able to keep down any liquids or soft foods at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Very little. I try, but then the pain and heaving start. I’m not really vomiting food—just retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood when you vomit or in your stool? Any black, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. My bowel movements have been normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea, fevers, or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and prior anastomotic ulcers, we want to make sure there isn’t a new ulcer or narrowing at the connection. We’ll start with IV fluids tonight to treat dehydration and help your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is happening because I had the tube removed. Did I mess things up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You didn’t do anything wrong. Sometimes symptoms return after changes in how nutrition is supported, and sometimes irritation or reflux can flare. Our job now is to stabilize you and look for a treatable cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me in the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fluids, and we’re also planning a vitamin-containing infusion—often called a banana bag—because people with poor intake can get depleted. We’ll also check labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. First we’ll see if we can get you comfortable and tolerating a bariatric diet again. We’ll also plan an upper endoscopy to look at the pouch and connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was started on Carafate in clinic. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sucralfate, or Carafate, coats irritated areas. We’ll continue it here, and we’ll also increase acid suppression while you’re inpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My reflux has been awful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with what you’re describing. We’ll give pantoprazole through the IV twice a day for now, which is stronger and faster than pills when you’re not keeping things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having waves of pain. Can I have something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll treat pain, but we’ll do it carefully because stronger pain meds can worsen nausea. We’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and reassess often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after the fluids and medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still dry heaving, but not as constant. I’m exhausted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it eased some. Your vital signs have been stable. We’re going to start you on a stage 4 bariatric diet today—very gentle, small amounts—and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does stage 4 mean again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a soft, more advanced bariatric diet than clear liquids, but still easy to digest. The key is tiny portions, slow sips, and stopping before you feel full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start heaving again, does that mean something is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not automatically. Dry heaving can come from irritation, reflux, or sensitivity after bypass. The endoscopy will help us rule out a narrowing or ulcer at the connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down a little of the diet, but I’m scared to push it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach—don’t push. The goal today is tolerance without triggering symptoms. You’re also urinating well, which tells us hydration is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is the scope happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning it for tomorrow. You’ll need to be NPO—nothing by mouth—for a period beforehand. The team will give you exact timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What are you looking for exactly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look at the gastric pouch and the small intestine limbs created by the bypass, including the connections. We’re checking for ulcers, erosions, inflammation, or narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today is the endoscopy day. How are your symptoms right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pain, but less. The dry heaves are less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole going. After the procedure, we’ll decide whether to switch back to pills and advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and usually don’t remember much. It’s done through the mouth with a camera; no incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the endoscopy. It went smoothly. Want to hear what we found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Is there an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is the bypass anatomy looked as expected. The blind limb looked unremarkable, and the alimentary limb and the jejuno-jejunal connection looked unremarkable. We did see a small erosion in the cardia area of the gastric remnant/pouch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a big ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—this was described as a small erosion, not a large ulcer, and there was no mention of a blockage. That fits with irritation and reflux-type symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes an erosion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often acid exposure and irritation. After bariatric surgery, the anatomy changes and the lining can be more sensitive. That’s why we’re focusing on strong acid suppression and sucralfate to protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart with your bariatric diet and advance as tolerated. Start slow. If you can keep it down without worsening symptoms, that’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the dry heaves will come back when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid worry. We’ll send you home on pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day. We’ll also give you metoclopramide to use as needed for nausea, and a short course of pain medication for the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pantoprazole twice a day—wasn’t I on it once a day before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given the erosion and your symptoms, we’re increasing it to twice daily to better control acid and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you do overnight with eating and drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had small amounts and didn’t dry heave as much. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re tolerating a stage 5 bariatric diet now, you’re walking around, and you’re urinating without trouble. Those are the main discharge goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What is stage 5 compared to stage 4?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stage 5 is a step up—more regular textured bariatric foods, still focusing on small portions and avoiding anything that triggers reflux or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My labs—are they okay? I’m always worried about being malnourished again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this stay were overall reassuring—kidney function and electrolytes looked stable, and your blood counts were acceptable though on the lower side earlier. The bigger issue is making sure you can maintain intake at home, and we’ll give you clear return precautions if you can’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking all my other meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications unless we specifically changed them. The key changes are pantoprazole now twice daily and continuing sucralfate. Metoclopramide is as needed for nausea, and lorazepam is as needed for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back if you can’t keep down fluids or medications, if you feel dehydrated—dry mouth, fast heartbeat, dizziness when standing—if you vomit blood or see black stools, if you have worsening pain, chest symptoms, shortness of breath, or fever over 101.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive myself home if I’m taking pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—don’t drive or operate machinery while taking pain medication. Arrange a ride today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to avoid lifting or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon. Also rest, walk several times a day, and focus on hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the plan is just meds and diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Since the endoscopy didn’t show a blockage and only a small erosion, the treatment is medical: acid suppression with pantoprazole twice daily, mucosal protection with sucralfate, and careful bariatric diet progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel better knowing it wasn’t something severe. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork now and make sure you understand the medication schedule and follow-up instructions before you leave.
